summary: Register your address at the local municipal office (City or Ward Hall) within 14 days of moving into your residence in Japan.
details: Upon arrival at Narita, Haneda, Kansai, or Chubu airports, mid-to-long term students receive a Residence Card (Zairyu Card). You must take this card to the local municipal office (shiyakusho or kuyakusho) within 14 days of finding an address. Fill out the Moving-in Notification (Tennyu-todoke / 転入届). Bring your passport, residence card, and lease or dormitory agreement. This also initiates your National Health Insurance and My Number registration.
useful_phrases: 住所の登録をしたいです (Jusho no toroku o shitai desu - I want to register my address) / 転入届を出したいです (Tennyu-todoke o dashitai desu - I want to submit a moving-in notification)

summary: Opening a bank account in Japan for students
details: usually at Japan Post Bank (Yucho Ginko) or Shinsei Bank.
useful_phrases: Most traditional Japanese banks (MUFG, SMBC, Mizuho) require 6 months of residency in Japan before opening a standard account. However, Japan Post Bank (Yucho Ginko / ゆうちょ銀行) allows new international students to open an account immediately. Required documents: Residence Card, Student ID, Passport, Japanese phone number, and a Hanko (or signature for Yucho). Yucho provides a cash card and passbook. Online banks like Sony Bank or SBI Shinsei Bank also offer English support.
column7: 口座を開設したいです (Koza o kaisetsu shitai desu - I would like to open an account) / 通帳 (Tsucho - Bank passbook) / キャッシュカード (Kyasshu kaado - Cash card)

japanese_title: SIMカード・携帯電話契約
summary: Getting a Japanese phone number and mobile data plan.
details: A Japanese phone number (starting with 070, 080, or 090) is essential for bank accounts, city hall forms, and deliveries. Major low-cost carriers (MVNOs) popular with international students include ahamo (NTT Docomo), LINEMO (SoftBank), povo 2.0 (au), Rakuten Mobile, and student-friendly providers like Mobal and GTN Mobile that don't require a Japanese credit card. Bring your unlocked smartphone, Residence Card, and a credit or debit card for signing up.
useful_phrases: SIMカードを契約したいです (SIM kaado o keiyaku shitai desu - I want to contract a SIM card) / 携帯番号 (Keitai bango - Mobile number)

details: In Japan, a Hanko (personal seal) is traditionally used instead of signatures for legal, financial, and administrative documents. There are three types: Mitome-in (認め印, daily unregistered seal for packages and routine forms), Ginko-in (銀行印, registered with your bank), and Jitsuin (実印, officially registered at city hall for major contracts like apartment leases). As a foreigner, you can get a seal carved with your Katakana or English initials at seal shops (Hanko-ya) or automated seal machines (Don Quijote). While many services now accept signatures, having a Hanko is still highly recommended.
useful_phrases: 印鑑 (Inkan - Seal) / 判子 (Hanko - Stamp) / サインでもいいですか？ (Sain de mo ii desu ka? - Is a signature acceptable?)

summary: Mandatory health insurance for all residents in Japan
useful_phrases: All international students staying in Japan for more than 3 months must enroll in the National Health Insurance (Kokumin Kenko Hoken / 国保). You apply at the insurance division of your local city/ward hall. It covers 70% of medical and dental expenses; you only pay 30% out-of-pocket at clinics and hospitals. As a student with low or no income in Japan, you can apply for a significant premium reduction (Gakusei Menjo). Carry your physical health insurance card (Hokensho) whenever visiting a doctor.
column7: 保険証 (Hokensho - Health insurance card) / 学生割引・減額申請 (Gakusei waribiki / gengaku shinsei - Student premium reduction application)

details: Every resident receives a 12-digit Individual Number (My Number). You will first receive a paper Notification Card by registered mail. You can then apply online or at city hall for the plastic My Number Card equipped with an IC chip and photo. The card is useful for identity verification, printing official certificates (like Juminhyo) at convenience stores for half price, tax procedures, and opening financial accounts.
useful_phrases: マイナンバー (Mai Nambaa - My Number) / 住民票 (Juminhyo - Certificate of residence)

summary: Permission to work part-time up to 28 hours per week on a student visa.
details: Student visa holders are not automatically permitted to work. You must obtain 'Permission to Engage in Activity Other than that Permitted under the Status of Residence' (Shikakugai Katsudo Kyoka / 資格外活動許可). You can apply for this at the airport immigration counter upon arrival or later at an Regional Immigration Bureau. Once granted (indicated by a stamp on the back of your Residence Card), you may work up to 28 hours per week during school terms, and up to 8 hours per day during official school vacation periods. Working in adult entertainment or gambling establishments is strictly prohibited.
useful_phrases: 資格外活動許可 (Shikakugai katsudo kyoka - Part-time work permit) / アルバイト (Arubaito - Part-time job)

summary: Disposal rules for burnable garbage including food waste and paper.
details: Combustible waste includes kitchen food scraps, contaminated paper, wooden items, cooking oil absorbed in paper/solidified, and clothing. Drain all excess water from food scraps before bagging. In Tokyo 23 wards, use standard transparent or semi-transparent 45L bags. In cities like Kyoto or Machida, use yellow designated municipal bags (Shitei gomibukuro). Collection is typically 2 to 3 times per week in the morning before 8:00 AM at your designated neighborhood collection point (Gomi-shusekisho).
useful_phrases: 生ごみ (Nama-gomi - Food scraps) / 水切りをしてください (Mizukiri o shite kudasai - Please squeeze out excess water)

japanese_title: 不燃ごみ (もえないごみ)
summary: Disposal rules for non-burnable household items.
details: Incombustible items include ceramic dishes, pottery, glassware, small metal utensils, light bulbs, umbrellas, and small household electronics. Wrap broken glass, needles, or sharp items in thick paper/cardboard and label clearly with 'KIKEN' (危険 - Danger) before putting into the transparent bag. Collected usually twice a month or once every two weeks.
useful_phrases: 危険 (Kiken - Danger / Broken glass) / 割れ物 (Waremono - Fragile items)

japanese_title: 資源ごみ・ペットボトル
summary: Correct recycling procedures for PET bottles
column7: PET bottles must have caps and plastic labels removed (throw cap and label into plastic packaging waste). Rinse the inside thoroughly with water, flatten lightly, and place in the designated net or container on collection day. Cans (aluminum and steel) should be rinsed clean. Glass beverage and food bottles should be rinsed; do not place broken glass in recycling. Paper and cardboard must be flattened and tied securely with cross-shaped paper twine (do not use plastic tape).
column8: キャップとラベルを外してください (Kyappu to raberu o hazushite kudasai - Remove cap and label) / すすいでください (Susuide kudasai - Rinse inside)

summary: Procedures for disposing of large items exceeding 30cm.
details: Items larger than 30 cm (furniture, suitcases, futons, bicycles, desk chairs) cannot be thrown in regular garbage. You must: 1. Apply online or by phone with your ward's Sodai Gomi Center. 2. Purchase the specified fee sticker (Sodai Gomi Shorisou-ken / 粗大ごみ処理券) at any convenience store. 3. Affix the sticker with your name/application number. 4. Place the item outside your residence by 8:00 AM on the scheduled pickup date. Home appliances like refrigerators, TVs, washing machines, and air conditioners follow the Home Appliance Recycling Law and cannot be collected as bulky waste.
useful_phrases: 粗大ごみ受付センター (Sodai gomi uketsuke sentaa - Bulky waste reception center) / 処理券 (Shori-ken - Disposal fee sticker)

summary: Proper disposal of dry cell batteries
column7: Dry cell batteries (alkaline/manganese) are placed in transparent bags on designated hazardous waste days or dropped into collection boxes at electronics stores and municipal ward offices. Lithium-ion rechargeable batteries must be returned to collection bins at electronics stores (Bic Camera, Yodobashi). Gas cartridges and aerosol spray cans must be completely emptied outdoors in a well-ventilated area until no hissing sound remains; some wards require puncturing a hole, while others forbid puncturing—always check your local municipal guideline.
column8: 中身を使い切ってください (Nakami o tsukaikitte kudasai - Use up contents completely) / 乾電池回収ボックス (Kandenchi kaishu bokkusu - Battery collection box)

column7: For Crime, Accidents, or Violence: Call 110 (Police / Keisatsu). For Fire or Medical Emergencies: Call 119 (Ambulance / Kyukyusha, Fire / Shobosha). The operators speak Japanese; clearly say 'Kyukyusha onegaishimasu' for an ambulance or 'Kaji desu' for fire. If you cannot speak Japanese, say 'English please' as multi-language interpretation is available in major cities. For non-emergency medical consultation when unsure whether to call an ambulance, dial #7119 (Tokyo and major regions).
column8: 救急車をお願いします (Kyukyusha o onegaishimasu - Please send an ambulance) / 警察を呼んでください (Keisatsu o yonde kudasai - Please call the police)

japanese_title: 病院・クリニックの受診
summary: How to visit medical facilities in Japan with National Health Insurance.
details: In Japan, for general illnesses (cold, fever, stomach ache), first visit a local neighborhood clinic (Iin or Kurinikku) rather than a large general hospital (which charges a high first-visit fee without a referral letter). Walk into the reception, present your Health Insurance Card (Hokensho), and fill out the medical questionnaire (Monshinhyo / 問診票). After consultation, pay at the counter (30% of total cost) and take the prescription (Shohosen) to any nearby dispensing pharmacy (Chouzai Yakkyoku) to receive your medication.
useful_phrases: 熱があります (Netsu ga arimasu - I have a fever) / お腹が痛いです (Onaka ga itai desu - My stomach hurts) / 処方箋 (Shohosen - Prescription)

summary: Essential everyday utilities available at Japanese convenience stores (Combini).
details: Japanese convenience stores (7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Lawson) offer far more than snacks: 1. Multi-function copy machines for printing documents, photos, and official certificates (Juminhyo via My Number). 2. Bill Payment (Shunou-hyo) for utility bills (electricity, water, gas), National Health Insurance, and online purchases by paying cash at the register. 3. ATMs that accept international cards (especially 7-Bank ATMs). 4. Delivery parcel pickup and sending (Ta-Q-Bin). 5. Ticket purchasing for concerts, museums (Ghibli Museum), and highway buses.
useful_phrases: 温めてください (Atatamete kudasai - Please warm this up) / 袋はいりません (Fukuro wa irimasen - I don't need a plastic bag) / レシートは結構です (Reshiito wa kekko desu - No receipt needed)

summary: Rules for riding trains and subways in Japanese cities.
details: 1. Switch your smartphone to 'Manner Mode' (silent) and refrain from talking on the phone. 2. Keep your backpack on your front or place it on the overhead luggage rack during crowded times. 3. Respect Priority Seats (Yusen-seki) designated for elderly, pregnant women, and injured passengers. 4. Wait in designated queues behind the platform line until passengers have fully exited the train before boarding. 5. Avoid eating or drinking smelly foods on commuter trains.
useful_phrases: マナーモード (Manaa moodo - Silent mode) / 優先席 (Yusen-seki - Priority seating) / 降車優先 (Kosha yusen - Let passengers off first)

japanese_title: 地震・防災マニュアル
summary: Disaster preparedness steps and emergency actions in Japan.
details: Japan experiences frequent earthquakes. Follow these key safety guidelines: 1. 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On' under a sturdy table or desk until shaking stops. Protect your head with a pillow or bag. 2. Extinguish open cooking fires once shaking subsides. 3. Keep shoes near your bed in case of broken glass. 4. Learn your neighborhood Evacuation Area (Hinan-jo / 避難所), usually the nearest public elementary or junior high school. 5. If phone networks fail, use NTT's Disaster Emergency Message Dial: call 171 and follow recorded guidance to leave a voice message using your phone number.
useful_phrases: 避難所 (Hinan-jo - Evacuation shelter) / 地震 (Jishin - Earthquake) / 津波警報 (Tsunami keiho - Tsunami warning) / 災害用伝言ダイヤル 171 (Saigai-yo dengon daiyaru - Emergency message service 171)

japanese_title: 学生のための基本日本語
summary: Crucial everyday conversational phrases for study
column7: Essential phrases: 'Konnichiwa' (Hello), 'Arigatou gozaimasu' (Thank you very much), 'Sumimasen' (Excuse me / Sorry), 'Onegaishimasu' (Please), 'Kore wa ikura desu ka?' (How much is this?), 'Eigo ga hanasemasu ka?' (Can you speak English?), 'Wakarimasen' (I don't understand), 'Kore o kudasai' (Please give me this), 'Toire wa doko desu ka?' (Where is the restroom?), 'Daijoubu desu' (It's okay / No thank you).
column8: ありがとうございます (Arigatou gozaimasu - Thank you very much) / すみません (Sumimasen - Excuse me / Sorry) / お願いします (Onegaishimasu - Please) / これをください (Kore o kudasai - I will take this)
